chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ismail ibn Marar, from Yunus, from one of our companions, who said:
I asked him about the Words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: 'So do not swear by the places of the stars.' He said: 'I consider it a great sin for the one who swears by it.'
And the people of the Pre-Islamic period revered the Sanctuary (Mecca) and did not swear by it, permitting the sanctity of Allah within it, and did not expel an animal from it.
So Allah, Blessed and High, said: 'Indeed! I swear by this city, And you are a dweller of this city, And father and son.'
They revered the city if they were to swear by it, and they permitted in it the violation of the sanctity of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family).

key_terms.مَواقِعِ النُّمُورِ: Places of the stars (referring to their positions in the sky)

ai.seo_question: Why did the Pre-Islamic Arabs not swear by the Kaaba according to Shia interpretation?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi elucidates the theological principle that while Allah swears by Mecca to emphasize its sanctity, the Pre-Islamic Arabs (Ahl al-Jahiliyyah) revered the city but violated its sanctity by swearing by other entities like stars or the Prophet himself. It highlights the transition from idolatrous oaths to monotheistic affirmation, noting that swearing by the Prophet or celestial bodies constitutes a grave sin because it attributes divine authority to creation rather than the Creator. This reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on Tawhid in speech and practice, distinguishing between Allah's unique right to swear and human misuse of sacred symbols.
